I am still doing wheat-maize on all 10.1 mu. At my age, and with only two people in the household, I do not want fancy changes. What has kept my land steady is winter wheat first, then summer maize right after harvest. I have enough experience to know that if I miss the maize window, I lose more than I gain from extra tillage, so I will keep the turnaround tight. I do read the crop condition and soil better than before, so I split fertilizer instead of putting everything at once, but I still make decisions the farmer's way: what worked on my own fields, what the neighbors are doing, and what I can pay for without making the household too tight on cash.

For wheat, I want a stable stand and decent tillering, so I will sow in early October with a reliable improved variety, not the cheapest seed but not an expensive specialty one either. I will put most of the phosphorus and potassium down as base fertilizer, then split nitrogen between base and jointing. Since I have well water, I will irrigate wheat three times if the year is normal: once after sowing if the soil is dry, once at jointing, and once around grain filling if needed. For maize, I will plant immediately after wheat harvest in mid-June, using hybrid seed because maize seed quality shows up directly in yield. I will not waste time on deep tillage between crops; I will use shallow rotary tillage or direct seeding after residue handling so I do not lose moisture or the planting window. I will fertilize maize in two steps, give it one irrigation around big flare or tasseling if rain is short, and keep pesticide use practical, only what is needed for weeds and insects. I am aiming for steady yield, not the highest possible yield, because pumping water and buying too much fertilizer costs real money.
